messages.author: c6e5a5622337843b
messages.subject: Problems with interpreting a variogram
parts:
Hello all, 

I am a bit at a loss in interpreting an empirical variogram of a forest bird we tracked for a couple of hours using a VHF transmitter. We tracked this bird and a handful of others continuously in bouts of 3 hours every day -  either (or ideally) in the morning (8-11 am), mid-afternoon (11 -14 pm), or afternoon ( 14-17 pm). We aimed to track them for a minimum of 27 hours), but this was not always possible because some birds lost the transmitter along the way or the transmitter's battery died.

These birds are known to be territorial and have high site fidelity. Is there an asymptote in this variogram I have attached here?  Also, what could explain the abrupt peaks and valleys in the variogram for this individual? Is it safe to calculate home ranges for this individual?

Thank you in advance for your assistance.
Gladys.

This is from gaps in the data. You should try the dt argument highlighted in the vignette.

messages.author: c6e5a5622337843b
messages.subject: Re: [ctmm-user] Re: Problems with interpreting a variogram
parts:
Dear Christen,

Thank you very much for getting back to me so quickly. I have tried to play around with 'dt,' but I have not got around to it as yet, that is, specifying the right time-lag bin width. Our sampling regime was irregular because we took GPS fixes every time the birds moved - that is, once we spotted the bird, we recorded the time, watched its activity at a safe distance and then took GPS coordinates once it moved to another foraging patch. I have, however, used the shiny APP to check the variogram for this individual, and this is what it looks like (attached photo).

The effective sample size for this individual is 15, and the absolute sample size is 47 ( it was spending a lot of time in each foraging patch). This individual was tracked for 18 hours ( that is within 6 days, for 3 hours each day). Given that the variogram somehow flattens with an increasing time lag, am I right to say that this bird has been tracked 'enough' to show range residency, and thus we can calculate home ranges?
I will highly appreciate your thoughts.

Thank you,
Gladys.

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: [ctmm-user] Re: Problems with interpreting a variogram
parts:
Hi Gladys,

That sounds like I would try something like dt=c(MEDIAN,3%#%'hr',1%#%'day') where MEDIAN is the median sampling interval.
The second variogram looks range resident, in as much as I can see, but it can be cleaned up.

Best,
Chris
